title: Regulation of alternative polyadenylation in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae by histone H3K4 and H3K36 methyltransferases.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the full Europe PMC supplementary archive (1.6 MB): it holds 16 figure images (.jpg/.gif) plus one 99 KB PDF. I extracted the PDF text with pypdf — 4 pages, three supplementary figures of bar graphs and their legends, zero data tables. I searched the whole open-access full text (100 KB dump) for GSE/SRP/PRJNA/'Gene Expression Omnibus'/'deposited' — none present outside the reference list; the only text-mined 'accessions' are two DOIs of cited papers. NCBI elink from the PubMed ID returned only related PMC articles, no GEO, SRA, BioProject, BioSample or dbGaP records, and the Zenodo/Dryad DOI search returned nothing.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The experimental design (which strains, which genes, how many biological replicates) comes from the methods text and figure legends. I did not try to digitize values off the bar-chart images.

a1_downloadable.note: FAIL. There is no dataset of any kind. The only downloadable items are figure images and a 4-page supplementary PDF of bar graphs; no GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus), SRA (Sequence Read Archive), BioProject, Zenodo or Dryad record exists for this paper. Europe PMC's 'hasData' flag is a false positive.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. The quantity a model would predict (long-isoform / total mRNA ratio per gene per strain) exists only as bar heights inside figure images. It would have to be constructed by eyeballing or digitizing plots, which is the clearest possible A2 failure.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAIL. No sequences, coordinates or feature tables are supplied. Polyadenylation site positions are quoted from a cited paper (Graber et al. 2013), and only as star marks drawn on gene cartoons; qPCR primer sequences (Table 3) are the only sequence data in the paper.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated on the figure axes ('Long / Total mRNA', 'mRNA normalized to 18S', ChIP signal as percent input) and in the methods. This is the one killer the paper passes, but it is moot with no file to put them in.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. Roughly 10 genes (ISM1, FAT1, MDV1, RRD2, RTG2, GRS2, RAD53, RPB2, PDC1, RPP1B) across about 6 strains, 3 biological replicates each — on the order of 100-200 individual qPCR measurements, far under the ~400-row floor, and none of them in a machine-readable form.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small, but small because there is nothing there.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Not assessable: there is no file whose row count could be compared with the paper.

a8_label_provenance.note: Provenance of the measurements themselves is clean — quantitative reverse-transcription PCR of long versus total mRNA isoforms, a direct physical measurement, not another model's output. Irrelevant given A1/A2/A3/A5 fail.

existing_models.name: PolyaStrength / PolyaClassifier (Genome Research 2024, 'Delineating yeast cleavage and polyadenylation signals using deep learning')
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on 40,453 top-expressed cleavage sites across 5,491 Saccharomyces cerevisiae genes, predicting site isoform ratio on a log-odds scale from 500-nucleotide sequence windows; exact held-out metric read from the search summary only, not from the paper itself.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved — I read the search summary, not the full paper.

existing_models.name: APARENT / APARENT2 (Bogard et al., Cell 2019; Linder et al., Genome Biology 2022), deep neural networks for human alternative polyadenylation
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on >3 million randomized 3' untranslated region polyadenylation reporters in human HEK293 cells; base-pair-resolution cleavage prediction. Numbers taken from search summaries, not verified in the papers.

existing_models.name: DeeReCT-APA, a deep learning model of alternative polyadenylation site usage
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved beyond the title; listed here only to show the task is actively modelled.

backbone.name: Not applicable — no data to fit a head on. (Had data existed, a DNA language model such as Nucleotide Transformer or DNABERT-2 on sequence around polyadenylation sites would have been the natural choice.)

integration.partner_dataset: None usable. In principle the yeast 3'-end sequencing atlas behind PolyaStrength, or Graber et al. 2013 poly(A) site maps, joinable on systematic yeast gene name plus chromosomal coordinate — but this paper contributes no rows to join.
integration.join_key: Saccharomyces Genome Database systematic gene name (e.g. YDR180W) / genome coordinates, sacCer3 build
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written usefully: the paper supplies ~10 genes, so any join would be a lookup, not a dataset.

controls.positive_control: Would have been recovering the known U-rich / UA-rich efficiency element grammar upstream of yeast poly(A) sites. Not runnable here.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling — not runnable, no labels in machine-readable form.
controls.external_validation: The published yeast 3'-end sequencing data used by PolyaStrength would have served, but it would supply both training and test data, making this paper redundant.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is available: with about ten genes measured by quantitative PCR and no deposited table, any model fitted here would be describing bar-chart heights, not biology.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use DNA sequence around yeast polyadenylation sites to predict how a chromatin-modifying enzyme deletion shifts which site is used.
plain_idea.train_on: Intended inputs: sequence and chromatin context around each candidate polyadenylation site in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Verified example count available from this paper: about 10 genes, not thousands.
plain_idea.predict: Intended output: the shift in long-isoform fraction between wild-type and set1-deleted or set2-deleted cells. The true answer here comes from quantitative reverse-transcription PCR on long versus total mRNA, reported only as bar graphs.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: If it worked at genome scale it would tell RNA-processing labs which genes switch polyadenylation site under nutrient stress, but this paper provides nowhere near enough measurements to attempt it.

more_or_better_data.why: This paper offers ~10 genes measured by quantitative PCR; the 2024 yeast deep learning study (PolyaStrength) already used 40,453 cleavage sites across 5,491 yeast genes from 3'-end sequencing.

confidence_score.why: Three biological replicates per gene exist, which in principle estimates noise, but the replicate values are not released — only means with standard-deviation error bars drawn in figures.

models_beatable.why: The nearest competitor is a 2024 convolutional-recurrent network trained on tens of thousands of sites with open code; nothing in this paper could be used to challenge it.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition: our side of the comparison has no feature/label table at all, so the existing model cannot be run as a baseline against anything.

ml_idea: The only idea the paper supports is a genome-wide model of how loss of the histone methyltransferases Set1 or Set2 shifts polyadenylation site choice — but that needs 3'-end sequencing of the mutants, which this study never performed and never deposited. The idea belongs to the datasets behind PolyaStrength (Genome Research 2024) and Graber et al. 2013, not to this paper.

effort.compute_note: No compute estimate is meaningful: the entire supplement is 1.6 MB of images and a 4-page PDF, with no tabular data to load.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: List the supplementary files and grep the full text for a GEO/SRA accession — five minutes, and it kills the project: there is no accession and no data table anywhere.

verdict_reason: Part A1 fails outright: this is a targeted molecular-biology paper with no deposited data. The only downloadable items are 16 figure images and a 99 KB supplementary PDF of bar graphs, which I opened and read; no GEO, SRA, BioProject, Zenodo or Dryad record exists for the DOI or the PubMed ID. A2 fails as well — the quantity to predict (long/total mRNA isoform ratio) exists only as bar heights — and A5 fails by two orders of magnitude, with roughly ten genes across six strains at three replicates each. Separately, the task is already served by open models trained on far more data (PolyaStrength, Genome Research 2024, on 40,453 yeast cleavage sites; APARENT2 for human).
